slides.title: A probability experiment
slides.body: A probability experiment produces an outcome that is uncertain before it occurs.
slides.question: What are the possible outcomes when a fair six-sided die is rolled?

slides.title: Sample space
slides.body: The sample space contains all possible outcomes.
slides.question: What sample space describes two ordered tosses of a fair coin?

slides.title: An event
slides.body: An event is a set of outcomes from the sample space.
slides.question: For a die roll, what outcomes belong to “an even number”?

slides.title: Equally likely outcomes
slides.body: If all outcomes are equally likely, event probability is favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
slides.question: What is the probability of a value greater than 4 on a fair six-sided die?

slides.title: Unequal probabilities
slides.body: A spinner has a red region covering half the circle and two other regions covering one quarter each.
slides.question: Are its three color outcomes equally likely?

slides.title: Probability bounds
slides.body: An event probability lies between 0 and 1.
slides.question: What do probabilities 0 and 1 mean?

slides.title: Relative frequency
slides.body: Synthetic simulation: 124 heads in 250 independent fair-coin tosses.
slides.question: What is the observed relative frequency of heads?

slides.title: Long-run behavior
slides.body: A fair coin has probability 0.5 of heads on each independent toss.
slides.question: Must the first ten tosses include exactly five heads?

slides.title: A complement
slides.body: The complement of A contains outcomes outside A.
slides.question: If P(A) = 0.35, what is P(A-complement)?

slides.title: Translate “not”
slides.body: A fair six-sided die is rolled. A is “roll a 6.”
slides.question: What outcomes belong to A-complement?

slides.title: The intersection
slides.body: A AND B means both events occur.
slides.question: For a fair die, A = even and B = greater than 3. Which outcomes belong to A AND B?

slides.title: The union
slides.body: A OR B means A occurs, B occurs, or both occur.
slides.question: For a fair die, A = even and B = greater than 3. Which outcomes belong to A OR B?

slides.title: Inclusive “or”
slides.body: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck.
slides.question: Does “a heart or a king” include the king of hearts?

slides.title: Conditional probability
slides.body: P(A | B) is the probability of A when the outcome is restricted to B.
slides.question: For a fair die, what is P(even | greater than 3)?

slides.title: The conditioned group
slides.body: Synthetic survey: 20 students use tablets; 8 of those also use laptops. Select one student uniformly from the tablet users.
slides.question: What is the denominator for P(laptop | tablet)?

slides.title: Reverse the condition
slides.body: Synthetic survey: 20 tablet users, 30 laptop users, and 8 use both. Select one of these surveyed students uniformly.
slides.question: Is P(laptop | tablet) equal to P(tablet | laptop)?

slides.title: Without replacement
slides.body: A box holds 3 red and 2 blue tokens. Draw one token, keep it, then draw another.
slides.question: How does the first draw affect the possible second draw?

slides.title: Write a probability event
slides.body: Let X be the number of heads in three independent fair-coin tosses.
slides.question: How would you write “at least two heads” using X?

slides.title: Independent events
slides.body: A and B are independent when knowing B does not change the probability of A, provided P(B) > 0.
slides.question: Would the first toss of a fair coin change the chance of heads on a separate independent toss?

slides.title: Test independence
slides.question: Are A and B independent?

slides.title: Dependence
slides.body: P(A) = 0.4 and P(A | B) = 0.7, with P(B) > 0.
slides.question: What does knowing B change?

slides.title: Independent product
slides.body: Two printers operate independently. Their probabilities of completing a job without a jam are 0.9 and 0.8.
slides.question: What is the probability both complete without a jam?

slides.title: Two successes
slides.body: Two independent fair-coin tosses are made.
slides.question: What is the probability of heads on both tosses?

slides.title: Two outcomes in one roll
slides.body: A fair die is rolled. A = even; B = greater than 3.
slides.question: Are A and B independent?

slides.title: Mutually exclusive events
slides.body: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together in one experiment.
slides.question: On one die roll, are “a 2” and “a 5” mutually exclusive?

slides.title: Not mutually exclusive
slides.body: One card is drawn from a standard deck. A = heart; B = king.
slides.question: Can both events happen together?

slides.title: Positive-probability disjoint events
slides.body: A and B are mutually exclusive, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4.
slides.question: If B occurs, what is P(A | B)?

slides.title: Disjoint or independent?
slides.body: A and B are mutually exclusive and both have positive probability.
slides.question: Can A and B also be independent?

slides.title: With replacement
slides.body: A box contains 3 red and 2 blue tokens. Draw, replace, mix, and draw again uniformly.
slides.question: Are the two red-draw events independent?

slides.title: Without replacement
slides.body: A box contains 3 red and 2 blue tokens. Draw two uniformly without replacement.
slides.question: What is the probability of a red second draw given a red first draw?

slides.title: Which assumption fails?
slides.body: A student answers a series of questions while receiving coaching after every response.
slides.question: Why might a constant-probability independent-trial model be questionable?

slides.title: A conditional check
slides.body: P(A) = 0.25 and P(A | B) = 0.25, with P(B) > 0.
slides.question: What does this tell us about independence?

slides.title: Complementary events
slides.body: A has probability 0.6 and A-complement has probability 0.4.
slides.question: Are these events mutually exclusive, independent, or both?

slides.title: An independence model
slides.body: Two machines share the same power supply.
slides.question: What might make their failure events dependent?

slides.title: Empirical association
slides.body: Synthetic survey: 60% of all students use laptops, but 80% of tablet users do.
slides.question: Are laptop use and tablet use independent in these data?

slides.title: Coin tosses and “due” outcomes
slides.body: An independent fair coin has landed tails six times in a row.
slides.question: What is the probability of heads on the next toss?

slides.title: Trials versus events
slides.body: A single die roll has events A = even and B = odd.
slides.question: Why does using a fair die not make these two events independent?

slides.title: Prepare a repeated-trial model
slides.body: A binomial model requires independent trials with the same success probability.
slides.question: Which is closer: draws with replacement or draws without replacement from a small box?

slides.title: The addition rule
slides.body: The general addition rule subtracts the overlap counted in both events.
slides.question: If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A AND B) = 0.2, what is P(A OR B)?

slides.title: Why subtract the overlap?
slides.body: Synthetic survey: 40 laptop users, 25 tablet users, and 10 use both.
slides.question: What is wrong with adding 40 + 25 to count those using either device?

slides.title: A union from counts
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students: 40 use laptops, 25 use tablets, and 10 use both. Select one uniformly.
slides.question: What is the probability of laptop or tablet use?

slides.title: A disjoint union
slides.body: A fair six-sided die is rolled.
slides.question: What is the probability of rolling 1 or 6?

slides.title: Complement of a union
slides.question: What is the probability of neither A nor B?

slides.title: An intersection from a union
slides.question: What is P(A AND B)?

slides.title: The multiplication rule
slides.body: The general multiplication rule uses a conditional probability.
slides.question: If P(A) = 0.4 and P(B | A) = 0.3, what is P(A AND B)?

slides.title: A dependent product
slides.body: A box has 3 red and 2 blue tokens. Draw two uniformly without replacement.
slides.question: What is the probability both are red?

slides.title: A different order
slides.body: A box has 3 red and 2 blue tokens. Draw two uniformly without replacement.
slides.question: What is the probability the first is red and the second blue?

slides.title: Either order
slides.body: A box has 3 red and 2 blue tokens. Draw two uniformly without replacement.
slides.question: What is the probability of one red and one blue in either order?

slides.title: An independent product
slides.body: Two independent fair dice are rolled.
slides.question: What is the probability both show 6?

slides.title: At least one
slides.body: Two independent fair dice are rolled.
slides.question: What is the probability at least one shows 6?

slides.title: Exactly one
slides.body: Two independent fair dice are rolled.
slides.question: What is the probability exactly one shows 6?

slides.title: A conditional ratio
slides.body: Conditional probability uses the intersection divided by the probability of the conditioning event.
slides.question: If P(A AND B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.30, what is P(A | B)?

slides.title: A zero denominator
slides.question: Can the usual conditional-probability ratio define P(A | B)?

slides.title: Read the notation
slides.body: A = laptop use; B = tablet use.
slides.question: How would you describe P(A AND B) in words?

slides.title: Choose the rule
slides.body: A probability question asks whether at least one of two events occurs.
slides.question: Which rule naturally connects the event probabilities and their overlap?

slides.title: Check coherence
slides.body: A proposed model has P(A) = 0.2 and P(A AND B) = 0.3.
slides.question: Can these probabilities describe valid events?

slides.title: Three independent events
slides.body: Three independent transmissions each succeed with probability 0.9.
slides.question: What is the probability all three succeed?

slides.title: A complement shortcut
slides.body: Three independent transmissions each succeed with probability 0.9.
slides.question: What is the probability at least one fails?

slides.title: A contingency table
slides.body: A contingency table records counts for combinations of categorical variables.
slides.question: Which two variables organize this synthetic survey?

slides.title: A joint count
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students.
slides.question: How many students use both a tablet and a laptop?

slides.title: A marginal count
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students.
slides.question: How many students use a laptop, regardless of tablet use?

slides.title: A marginal probability
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from this synthetic survey.
slides.question: What is the probability of tablet use?

slides.title: A joint probability
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from this synthetic survey.
slides.question: What is the probability of tablet AND laptop use?

slides.title: A union probability
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from this synthetic survey.
slides.question: What is the probability of tablet OR laptop use?

slides.title: Neither category
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from this synthetic survey.
slides.question: What is the probability of neither tablet nor laptop use?

slides.title: Condition on a row
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from the tablet users in this synthetic survey.
slides.question: What is the probability of laptop use?

slides.title: Condition on a column
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from the laptop users in this synthetic survey.
slides.question: What is the probability of tablet use?

slides.title: Different denominators
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from this synthetic survey.
slides.question: Why do P(laptop | tablet) and P(tablet | laptop) have different denominators?

slides.title: An independence check
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from this synthetic survey.
slides.question: Are tablet use and laptop use independent in these data?

slides.title: Mutual exclusivity check
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students.
slides.question: Are tablet use and laptop use mutually exclusive?

slides.title: Complete the counts
slides.body: Synthetic survey table. Every student is in exactly one row and one column.
slides.question: What counts fill the missing cells?

slides.title: Percent of which group?
slides.body: Synthetic survey: 18 of 30 tablet users also use laptops; 18 of 60 laptop users also use tablets.
slides.question: Which statement corresponds to 60%?

slides.title: A dependent table
slides.body: Select one student uniformly from this synthetic survey.
slides.question: Does tablet use change the probability of laptop use?

slides.title: Scope of the table
slides.body: A convenience survey finds laptop use and tablet use independent among respondents.
slides.question: Does this establish independence for all students at the college?

slides.title: A tree diagram
slides.body: A tree diagram represents a sequence of outcomes with branches.
slides.question: What two first branches represent one fair-coin toss?

slides.title: Build a two-stage tree
slides.body: Toss a fair coin twice independently.
slides.question: How would you label every branch and terminal outcome?

slides.title: Multiply along a path
slides.body: Two independent fair-coin tosses.
slides.question: What is the probability of the H then T path?

slides.title: Add terminal paths
slides.body: Two independent fair-coin tosses.
slides.question: Which paths contribute to exactly one head?

slides.title: Tree without replacement
slides.body: 3 red, 2 blue; uniform draws, no replacement.
slides.question: Why is P(red second | red first) = 2/4?

slides.title: A second set of branches
slides.body: 3 red, 2 blue; uniform draws, no replacement.
slides.question: What is the probability of the B then R path?

slides.title: Branch totals
slides.body: A tree node has outgoing probabilities 0.3, 0.4, and 0.4 for mutually exclusive exhaustive outcomes.
slides.question: What is wrong with this node?

slides.title: A tree with replacement
slides.body: A box holds 3 red and 2 blue tokens. Replace and mix after each uniform draw.
slides.question: How do the second-stage branch labels differ from drawing without replacement?

slides.title: A weighted path
slides.body: Synthetic model: 40% of jobs use server A, 60% use B; completion probabilities are 0.9 on A and 0.8 on B.
slides.question: What is the probability of choosing A and completing the job?

slides.title: Sum successful paths
slides.body: Synthetic model: 40% of jobs use server A, 60% use B; completion probabilities are 0.9 on A and 0.8 on B.
slides.question: What is the overall probability of completion?

slides.title: Reverse the conditioning
slides.body: Synthetic model: 40% of jobs use server A, 60% use B; completion probabilities are 0.9 on A and 0.8 on B.
slides.question: Given completion, what is the probability the job used A?

slides.title: A Venn diagram
slides.body: A Venn diagram places overlapping event regions inside the sample space.
slides.question: Where would an outcome belonging to both A and B appear?

slides.title: Fill the regions
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students: 60 use laptops, 30 use tablets, and 18 use both.
slides.question: What counts belong in the four regions of a two-circle Venn diagram?

slides.title: Only one category
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students.
slides.question: How many use a laptop but no tablet?

slides.title: Outside both circles
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students.
slides.question: How many use neither device?

slides.title: Shade a union
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students.
slides.question: Which regions form laptop OR tablet?

slides.title: Shade a complement
slides.body: Synthetic survey of 100 students.
slides.question: Which region complements laptop OR tablet?

slides.title: Disjoint circles
slides.body: Two positive-probability events have no overlap in a Venn diagram.
slides.question: What does this show, and does it establish independence?
